concept.name: Auction market theory
concept.definition: A framework for understanding markets as continuous two-way auctions whose purpose is to facilitate trade: price advertises opportunities, and the market auctions up to attract sellers and down to attract buyers until trade occurs. Its central tenet is that price and value are distinct — value is where the market spends time and does volume, and markets alternate between balance (agreement) and imbalance (repricing). It is an interpretive philosophy, not a predictive model.
concept.intuition: A market behaves like an auction house: it keeps moving the price until buyers and sellers both show up, then does most of its business there until something changes.
concept.mechanics: Practitioners classify market states as balance or imbalance, locate value via time/volume distributions (Market Profile being the standard tool), and frame decisions around acceptance versus rejection of prices away from established value.
concept.failure_modes: AMT is a lens, not a falsifiable system: its categories (value, balance, acceptance) are defined loosely enough that almost any price action can be narrated post hoc, so it cannot by itself generate testable predictions.
concept.misconceptions: Auction market theory is often conflated with Market Profile — the theory is the philosophy of how auctions seek value, while the profile is merely one data-organization tool used to observe it; neither claims markets must revert to value.
concept.example: After a news shock, price slices through the prior day's value area; an AMT trader reads the market as imbalanced and seeking a new value level, and watches for where two-sided trade and time begin to build again.
